newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-Dlr/mark seen sturdy over Q3, then softer.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Dlr/mark seen sturdy over Q3, then softer.

text.p: The dollar should continue to outshine the mark in the coming months, as Europe staggers toward monetary union and capital departs the continent in favor of richer U.S. yields, according to the latest Reuters quarterly survey of U.S. economists.

"These factors are likely to continue to push us up for a while, getting to a little bit higher level, which would be seen as excessive. Then we come down from there," said Chris Rupkey, financial economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.
Dollar/mark should plateau mid-year and gradually depreciate through 1998 and into 1999, according to a Reuters poll conducted between April 15 and April 17.

Average forecasts put the dollar at 1.7260 marks on June 30, slightly above its current level approaching 1.7200 marks. It is seen essentially steady through the third quarter, which is expected to conclude with the dollar standing at 1.7236 marks.

Questions about which nations will qualify and whether the new unit -- to be called the euro -- will be diluted by the softer currencies of Italy and Spain, among others, has bolstered the dollar as a haven from all the uncertainty.

"Monetary union I think is going to see capital flee Europe, if decisions are made on who's in and who's out and people realize it's going to go ahead on time," said David Gilmore, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
Going forward, the dollar could stumble if foreigners grow weary of financing the yawning U.S. current account deficit by recycling export-earned dollars into Treasury bonds.

"We're going to run into some problems sometime by the end of this year, if we continue to move up, in that the G7 (Group of Seven) doesn't want to see the dollar appreciate that much further," Rupkey said.
Analysts said European Economic and Monetary Union appears firmly on track, despite friction between potential members regarding who will be among the first to join the single currency.
But, given the relative strength of the U.S. economy compared to Germany's, capital flows should support dollar/mark into the fourth quarter, Gilmore said.
The dollar is expected to ease to 1.6881 marks by the end of December and is seen falling further to 1.6372 marks by the end of 1998, according to the poll.
